content: 1. Screening donated blood for transfusion-transmissible infections is a critical step in ensuring the safety of blood transfusions. This process involves testing for various pathogens to prevent the transmission of infectious diseases to recipients. 2. Zoulim et al. (2015) investigated the quantification of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in patients with chronic hepatitis B who were treated with entecavir, with or without tenofovir, as part of the BE-LOW study. Their findings highlighted the importance of HBsAg levels in monitoring treatment response. 3. Brunetto (2010) emphasized the evolving role of HBsAg as a biomarker in the management of chronic hepatitis B, providing insights into its utility in disease monitoring and treatment strategies. 4. Brakenhoff et al. (2023) demonstrated that end-of-treatment levels of HBsAg, HBc-related antigen (HBcrAg), and HBV RNA can predict the risk of off-treatment ALT flares in patients with chronic hepatitis B, underscoring the importance of these biomarkers in clinical decision-making. 5. Jeng et al. (2021) reported significant differences in HBsAg kinetics among patients experiencing two types of hepatitis B flares, with and without retreatment. This study highlighted the clinical implications of monitoring HBsAg dynamics during disease flares. 6. Van Bommel et al. (2023) conducted a multicenter randomized-controlled trial to evaluate the cessation of nucleos(t)ide analogues in HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B patients. Their findings provided evidence on the outcomes and risks associated with treatment withdrawal. 7. Sonneveld et al. (2023) found that lower pretreatment HBV DNA levels were associated with better off-treatment outcomes following nucleos(t)ide analogue withdrawal in HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B patients. This multicenter cohort study emphasized the prognostic value of baseline viral load. 8. Saldanha et al. (2001) conducted an international collaborative study to establish a World Health Organization international standard for hepatitis B virus DNA nucleic acid amplification techniques, which is crucial for standardizing diagnostic and research methodologies. 9. Brouwer et al. (2016) demonstrated that repeated measurements of HBsAg can identify carriers of inactive HBV during long-term follow-up, aiding in the differentiation of inactive carriers from those with active disease. 10. Liu et al. (2016) showed that serum levels of HBsAg and HBV DNA can predict inactive carriers with a low risk of disease progression, providing valuable tools for risk stratification in chronic hepatitis B management. 11. Lok et al. (2022) reviewed novel biomarkers in hepatitis B infection, highlighting advancements in diagnostic and prognostic tools that can improve patient care and treatment outcomes. 12. Testoni et al. (2019) found that serum HBcrAg correlates with covalently closed circular DNA transcriptional activity in chronic hepatitis B patients, offering insights into viral replication and disease activity. 13. Wallace et al. (2017) explored the social implications of hepatitis B infection in China, revealing the broader impact of the disease beyond its clinical aspects, including stigma and discrimination. 14. Tu et al. (2020) examined the lived experiences of individuals with chronic hepatitis B, emphasizing the need for a cure to address the multifaceted impacts of the disease on patients' lives. 15. Mokaya et al. (2018) conducted a systematic review on the stigma associated with hepatitis B virus infection, highlighting the need for interventions to address this significant barrier to care. 16. Freeland et al. (2022) assessed the discrimination faced by people with hepatitis B across multiple countries, identifying key informant perspectives on the unvirtuous cycle of stigma and its impact on health outcomes. 17. Anyiwe et al. (2023) systematically reviewed the effectiveness of social determinants of health-focused interventions for hepatitis B, emphasizing the importance of addressing social factors in disease management. 18. Scambler (2009) discussed health-related stigma, providing a sociological perspective on its impact on individuals with chronic illnesses, including hepatitis B. 19. Yang and Wu (2011) highlighted the discrimination against hepatitis B carriers in China, calling for policy changes to address this pervasive issue. 20. Kan et al. (2015) further explored the discrimination faced by individuals with hepatitis B in China, emphasizing the need for public health interventions to combat stigma. 21. Le et al. (2019) investigated the social determinants of stigma and discrimination in Vietnamese patients with chronic hepatitis B, identifying factors that contribute to these challenges. 22. Han et al. (2018) examined the experiences of discrimination among individuals with chronic hepatitis B in four provinces of China, providing insights into the regional variations in stigma. 23. Ghany and Lok (2022) discussed the concept of a functional cure for hepatitis B, emphasizing the need to silence covalently closed circular and integrated HBV DNA to achieve long-term disease control. 24. Kayesh et al. (2021) reviewed the role of toll-like receptor responses in hepatitis B virus infection and the potential of TLR agonists as immunomodulators for treating chronic hepatitis B. 25. WHO guidelines provide comprehensive recommendations for the prevention, care, and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis B infection, emphasizing evidence-based approaches to improve patient outcomes. 26. Tsochatzis et al. (2014) reviewed liver cirrhosis, discussing its pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, and management strategies. 27. EASL (2017) clinical practice guidelines on hepatitis B virus infection management provide evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring. 28. Goodman (2007) outlined grading and staging systems for inflammation and fibrosis in chronic liver diseases, which are essential for assessing disease severity and guiding treatment decisions. 29. EASL (2021) updated guidelines on non-invasive tests for evaluating liver disease severity and prognosis, highlighting advancements in diagnostic tools. 30. Wai et al. (2003) developed a simple non-invasive index to predict significant fibrosis and cirrhosis in patients with chronic hepatitis C, providing a valuable tool for clinical practice.
